findings.issue: Guard bypass. `_argument_runs` and `_substitution_runs_body` only ask how the carrying command treats its argument. They never ask where that command's OUTPUT goes. With an emitter as the carrier, the body is dropped as data even when the emitter's output is then run. Both guards' own direct readings refuse the quoted spelling of the same command. Notation in this return: FORCEPUSH is a force push of main, STASHDROP is a stash drop, KEYREAD is `cat` of an ssh private key; the literal spellings are left out because this repo's guards grade the return's own text. Measured with each guard's decide() in a scratch repo carrying a recorded trail. guard-history-rewrite: `echo "$(cat <<'EOF'` / FORCEPUSH / `EOF` / `)" | sh` was deny at base 1529df9d and is allow now. The direct `echo "FORCEPUSH" | sh` is still deny. git_invocations goes from the stash verb to [] for an `echo "$(cat <<'EOF' ...STASHDROP...)"` carrier whose output goes to `| sh`, `| bash`, `|& sh`, `> .git/hooks/pre-commit`, `>> <home>/.bashrc`, `> f; sh f`, `| tee .git/hooks/post-checkout` or `> >(sh)`. The direct-quoted twin of every row is still caught by `_printed`/`_output_runs`. guard-secrets-read: the same echo carrier with a KEYREAD body piped to sh was block and is allow now; the direct spelling still blocks. The emitter-output machinery cannot see the body because runnable() strips it before `_expand_printed` runs, so the heredoc spelling skips every output-run rule the guard has. This is not the stated KNOWN LIMIT, which is about a program that runs its operand. No row in hb9/hb11 covers a carrier whose output is run.
findings.resolution: Keep the body as shell unless the carrying command's clause ends at the substitution's closing quote. The remainder of that clause after the closing quote is the text on the lines after the terminator, up to the next `;`/`&&`/`||`/newline. If it has a pipe (`|`, `|&`), an output redirect (`>`, `>>`, `>|`) or a `>(`, return "shell". The narrower alternative is to apply that rule to emitters only (echo, printf, `cat` with a here-string), but those are the carriers `_printed` reads. Add deny rows to hb11 for `echo "$(...)" | sh`, `printf '%s' "$(...)" | bash`, `echo "$(...)" > .git/hooks/pre-commit` and `echo "$(...)" > >(sh)`. Add one deny each through guard-history-rewrite's decide (FORCEPUSH body) and guard-secrets-read's decide (KEYREAD body).

findings.issue: A program word that is an expansion now passes as a command that does not run its argument. `_NOT_LITERAL` is applied to `partial` only. `$SHELL -c "$(cat <<'EOF' ...)"`, `"$SHELL" -c ...` and `${BASH} -c ...` reach `_word_runs_argument` with a program `$SHELL`, which is in no table, so the body is data. Measured: guard-history-rewrite went from deny to allow on `$SHELL -c` with a STASHDROP body, and guard-secrets-read went from block to allow on `$SHELL -c` with a KEYREAD body. guard-secrets-read still blocks the direct `$SHELL -c "KEYREAD"`. The invariant says 'unless that command runs what it is handed', and a program the reader cannot name cannot be shown not to. `_runs_input` in guard-history-rewrite already treats a `$` or a backquote in rest[0] as a runner, for exactly this reason.
findings.resolution: In `_argument_runs`, after `program_candidates`, return True when `rest[0]` (and any candidate word) contains a character from `_NOT_LITERAL`, which matches `_runs_input`'s rule. Add `$SHELL -c "$(...)"` and `"${BASH}" -c "$(...)"` to hb11's runners.

findings.issue: The KNOWN LIMIT is judged differently per guard, and the comment states only one of the two. Before this diff the default was deny (two vouched carriers). Now it is allow, minus `_SHELL_PROGRAMS`/`_RUNS_AN_OPERAND`/interpreters, so the completeness of those lists decides denials. Shells that take `-c` or `/c` are missing: csh, tcsh, pwsh, powershell, cmd, nu. So are common operand runners: nix-shell --run, npx -c, entr -s, hyperfine, nodemon --exec, tar --to-command, rsync -e and psql. Each was measured as kept-as-shell at base and data now. For guard-history-rewrite this is acceptable: its direct reading of a quoted argument to these programs also allows ('a quoted argument was never a command'), so the heredoc spelling opens no new route. guard-secrets-read is different: its direct reading blocks `csh -c "KEYREAD"` and `nix-shell --run "KEYREAD"`, both measured, and the heredoc spelling of each is now allowed. The shared rule therefore makes the heredoc spelling a bypass of the stricter guard. The comment does not say this, and the filed outcome says secrets-read is narrowed only for a body written to a `.sh` file.
findings.resolution: Give `_word_runs_argument` its own tuple of argument-running shells: `_SHELL_PROGRAMS` plus csh, tcsh, pwsh, powershell, cmd, nu, xonsh, elvish and yash. A separate tuple leaves `is_shell` callers unchanged. Add the operand runners nix-shell, npx, entr, hyperfine, nodemon, tar and rsync to `_RUNS_AN_OPERAND`. Extend the KNOWN LIMIT comment to say that the limit widens guard-secrets-read relative to its quoted-text reading. Add at least one deny row through guard-secrets-read's decide (csh -c over a KEYREAD heredoc body) to a suite in this task's gate.

findings.issue: The lookbehind in `_PROGRAM_WORD` leaves out `=`, which the `\b` it replaced covered. `env --split-string=bash <<'EOF'` runs bash on the body. It was shell at base and is data now: measured deny to allow in guard-history-rewrite with a STASHDROP body. `_head_runs_body` does not recover it, because `_wrapper_rest` gives up on `--split-string=` and the fallback strips it. `x --shell=bash <<EOF` changed the same way.
findings.resolution: Add `=` to the `_PROGRAM_WORD` class. A file name after `=` (`--out=report.sh`) puts a dot before `sh`, not `=`, so hb6 stays data. Add `env --split-string=bash <<'EOF'` to hb7.

findings.issue: The comment justifies the `_PROGRAM_WORD` narrowing only for a body WRITTEN to `deploy.sh`. It also turns `./deploy.sh <<'EOF'`, a RUN of a shell script with the body on stdin, from shell into data in both guards: measured deny to allow and block to allow. `_head_runs_body`'s own docstring says 'a script reading its stdin is one `read` and `eval` from running it' for a shell, and `sh deploy.sh <<EOF` stays shell (hb7). No row pins `./deploy.sh <<EOF` either way, so the change is an unstated decision.
findings.resolution: Pick one and pin it in hb6/hb7. Either treat a program-position word with a shell-script extension (`.sh`, `.bash`, `.zsh`) as a shell in `_head_runs_body`, which is consistent with `sh deploy.sh` and keeps the redirect-target fix, or say in this comment that a directly executed `.sh` script reading stdin is graded as `./deploy.py` is.

findings.issue: The inherited hb4 comment says 'the substitution's output is text only to the two consumers vouched for. Every other enclosing command may run it', and hb4's title says 'any other consumer could run is still kept'. This diff replaced exactly that allow-list with the invariant, so both texts now describe code that no longer exists.
findings.resolution: Rewrite the comment and the check title to name the invariant above `_argument_runs`: the body is kept when the carrier runs its argument by one of the listed routes.

preExisting.issue: `sudo -s <<'EOF'` and `su - root <<'EOF'` feed the body to a shell, but both base and the new code read them as data. `_wrapper_rest` treats `-s` as a no-value flag, which leaves no program.
preExisting.resolution: Treat `sudo -s`/`sudo -i`, and `su` with no `-c`, as a shell in `_head_runs_body`.
